voiceover.text: Here's the arm we finished on, a lever pivoting at the elbow. You've been told to lift with your legs, not your back, but why does that make a lift safer? "Legs are stronger" isn't the answer. And if someone pushes you sideways with your feet together, then again with your feet wide apart, what changed? Biomechanics, the physics of movement, answers both.

Linear motion is the whole body travelling one way. Angular motion is rotation about an axis, and every joint action is angular. Most movement is general motion, both at once: your limbs rotate at the joints, and that carries your body forward. A body keeps doing what it's doing until a force acts, so a moving player is hard to stop. Force equals mass times acceleration, so to accelerate harder, push harder or carry less. And every action has an equal and opposite reaction. A sprinter pushes back into the blocks, and the ground pushes them forward.

The bone is the bar, the joint is the pivot, called the fulcrum, the muscle's pull is the effort, and the load is the resistance. Whatever sits in the middle names the class. Fulcrum in the middle is first class, like nodding your head. Resistance in the middle is second class, like rising onto your toes. Effort in the middle is third class, like a biceps curl, and that's most of the body. Here the biceps pulls five centimetres from the elbow, holding fifty newtons thirty-five centimetres out. It needs seven times that force, three hundred and fifty newtons. What it buys is speed and range at the hand.

Next, balance. Your centre of gravity is the point where your weight is balanced in every direction. The line of gravity drops straight down from it. Your base of support is the area inside your points of contact. You stay balanced while the line of gravity falls inside the base. Five things raise stability: a lower centre of gravity, a wider base, a line of gravity nearer the middle of the base, more mass, and more points of contact. That's what widening your feet changed. It made the base bigger.

scenes.title: when less stability is the point

voiceover.text: But more stability isn't always better, because stability resists any change in motion, including the one you want. A sprinter in the set position raises the centre of gravity and moves the line of gravity to the front edge of the base, on purpose. Being almost off balance forward is the fastest way to start.

scenes.title: force: make it, aim it, absorb it

voiceover.text: Force raises three questions: make it, aim it, absorb it. To make the most force, use summation of forces: body parts in sequence, largest to smallest, each starting as the last one peaks, like legs, hips, trunk, then arm in a throw. To aim it, think about where it's applied. Through the centre gives straight-line motion, and off centre gives spin. And to absorb it safely, spread it over a longer time and a larger area. Bending your knees as you land buys time, using those eccentric contractions. Landing on the whole foot spreads the area.

In water and air, the main resistance is drag, and the biggest part is form drag, from the shape you present. A swimmer whose legs sink shows a bigger front to the water, so the same speed costs more effort. Buoyancy, the upward push of the water, holds the body up.

scenes.title: safe lifting is a torque problem

voiceover.text: Now the lift. The danger is torque, the turning effect of a force, which is the force times its distance from the pivot. Take a ten-kilogram box, about a hundred newtons. Held against your body, twenty centimetres from your lower spine, that's twenty newton metres. At arm's length, sixty centimetres out, it's sixty, three times the turning effect on your lower back. So keep the load close. Bending your knees is what lets you get close, so the torque stays small. Then the gluteus maximus and quadriceps do the work across big synovial joints. Keep your feet apart, so the line of gravity stays inside the base. And step to turn, rather than twist.

The same principles make squatting and walking safer. In a squat, keep the line of gravity over the middle of the foot, and let the knees track over the toes, so the hinge isn't pushed sideways. In walking, the heel lands first and the foot rolls through to the toes, while the ankle, knee and hip bend slightly, spreading the impact over more time.

Biomechanics also makes movement more efficient, which means getting the result for the least energy. For a wheelchair user, the seat and axle position set the angle at which the arm meets the push rim. Set well, the shoulder works in its middle range, each stroke is longer and smoother, fewer strokes are needed, and the shoulder takes less repeated strain. A running prosthesis is shaped to store energy on landing and return it at push-off. The principles don't change. Only the body parts available to apply them do.
Two things to remember. You stay balanced while the line of gravity stays inside your base. And safe lifting is a torque problem, so keep the load close.

scenes.title: attempt one (the tackle and the blocks)

voiceover.text: Two exam questions. First. A rugby player is about to be hit side-on in a tackle. Outline two ways the player could increase their stability, and explain why a swimmer on the starting block leans to the front edge. Pause here to answer.

Lower the centre of gravity by bending the knees, and widen the base towards the hit, so the line of gravity stays inside it. More stability resists the tackle's change in motion. A swimmer wants a fast start, so she leans her line of gravity to the front edge on purpose. The classic mistake is saying lower is always better.
Second. Outline how biomechanical principles can be applied to enhance the safety of lifting a heavy object from the floor. Pause here to answer.

Make every point a principle plus a structure. Keep the load close, which cuts the torque on the lumbar spine. Widen the base, keeping the line of gravity inside it. Lift with hip and knee extension, so the gluteus maximus and quadriceps work across synovial joints. Apply force smoothly, and step to turn. The classic mistake is a safety slogan, with no principle and no structure.
So, for any movement, name the principle and the muscle, bone or joint it protects. And all of this needs fuel. Look at a working thigh muscle. Its oxygen comes all the way from your chest.
